## Chapter 1

Drifting in the dead-water of the fin-de-siècle—where not a breath stirred the air of education or fretted the torpor of self-content—one lived alone. Adams had long ceased to go into society; for years he had not dined out of his own house, and six months’ oblivion had amounted to newspaper-death. Yet a few doors always stood open without asking or apology: Hay’s; Lodge’s; and, by a singular turn of chance, that of Senator Cameron’s household, where an intimacy of years taught him the type that had most blocked his own path and most steadily governed the Union. In a small society such household ties became a force; sandwiched between Cameron, Hay, and Lodge, with Roosevelt crossing the threshold as though born to it, one’s house was bound to the Republican interest whether one liked it or not.

In February, 1893, Cameron took his family to a Southern plantation, whence Adams drifted on to Havana, back again to the island, and then north to the Exposition at Chicago. Early in June they all sailed for England, and by July were in Switzerland. On the 22d they drove the Furka, and in the afternoon dropped by rail into Lucerne.

Months of contact educate, if character has interest; and to Adams the Pennsylvania mind had a keenness of interest that dated back to Grant. Narrow as a kirk, shy of alien narrowness as a Yankee, self-limited like a Puritan farmer, it reasoned little, talked less, and in practical matters was the steadiest of American types. As an ally it was worth all the rest, for it understood its own class, who were always a majority, and dealt with them as no New Englander could. The machine it built worked by coarse means on coarse interests, but its practical success was the most curious subject of study in our politics. Adding paradox to paradox, Adams reached the conclusion that the very mixture of Cameron’s qualities and defects made him the most useful man in the Senate.

On nothing did Cameron more impress him than on the year’s great discussion—the question of silver. Adams had taken no interest in it save as a tedious hobby of a friend; but, forced to choose, he was sure to choose silver. Every political idea and prejudice he owned—strict construction, limited powers, the eighteenth century and its morals—held him to the silver standard and made a barrier against gold. He admitted all that could be said for gold as economy; he knew that his own interests lay with it; yet he had not taken politics for the pursuit of economy, nor could he bring himself to help banker or croupier load the dice. One law he never doubted—that masses of men follow interests in deciding morals; morality is a private and costly luxury; a popular vote decides the standard by the balance of interest. To him the interest was political: perhaps the last chance to stand up for George Washington and the Constitution of 1789.

Therefore the surprise was the greater when Cameron, whom the reformers had abused for a lifetime as the servant of corporate interest, stood out as the leading champion of silver in the East. The moral puzzle became grotesque. Adams’s interests were with gold, yet he supported silver; the reformers’ interests were with gold, and they said so, pursuing their interest avowedly into politics; Cameron’s interests had always been with corporations, yet he supported silver. Thus morality required that Adams be condemned for resisting his interest; that the reformers were virtuous in following theirs; and that Cameron was a scoundrel whatever he did. Granting that one of the three was a moral idiot, which was it?

The banks gave the answer in their own language. After talking silver all the morning with Cameron on the Furka, Adams reached Lucerne to find letters summoning him home at once, for the community was bankrupt and he was probably a beggar. He slept upon it like a good citizen, but, arriving at Quincy, learned the lesson more rapidly than he liked. The banks had lent him, with others, money of which he knew little, for which he was responsible, and which they could not pay; he refused to pay theirs, they refused to pay his; each wanted to help the other; both sat down on the banks and asked what the banks would do about it. Blindly some powerful energy was at work, mechanical and one, doing what nobody wanted done. Men died like flies under the strain; Boston grew haggard and thin. Adams alone waxed fat and was happy, for at last he had his world in hand; here was a force that would finish his education.

He found Brooks at Quincy, absorbed in the same perplexities. Brooks had worked out a law of history that civilization followed the exchanges; everything American became unstable, compelled to find a new equilibrium; paradox piled on paradox, the acceleration outran his calculations. He laid down, among others, that the disequilibrium between capital and labor pointed not to collectivism but to anarchism; and Henry, who loved a paradox, made note of it.

When the storm lightened, he fled to Chicago and stayed a fortnight absorbed. Education went mad. The silver question, thorny as it was, fell into plain words compared with problems of credit and exchange. Educational game started like rabbits from every building and ran out of sight among thousands before one could mark a burrow. The Exposition defied explanation; its scenic surprise lay not in its façades but in its being there at all, a Babel of ill-joined thoughts ruffling the Lakes since Noah’s Ark. Yet the American looked at home in it; if he had not done it himself, he knew how to have it done; perhaps next time he would insist on doing it and show his own faults; but, for the moment, he had leaped straight from Syracuse and Venice over London and New York to impose classical standards on plastic Chicago. One sat on the steps beneath Hunt’s dome almost as deeply as on those of Ara Cœli. Here was a breach of continuity! If real, the new world had taken a conscious twist toward ideals; one’s personal friends might yet come in winners.

The exhibits promised help. Railroads seemed finished save for multiplication; steamers—nearer a unity—ran the surest line of triangulation into the future; a pencil scratch, over Cunard plans, brought limit-curves toward 1927. Explosives taught most, but wanted a tribe of specialists; the dynamo, still an infant, taught least, yet took the historian longest, for it gave history a new phase. Naïf as any savage, he asked what it was: did it pull or push? flow or vibrate? Was it a wire or a mathematical line? Men of science wondered at the questions and gave no answers. The historical mind, which can think only in historical processes, sat helpless, for its single clue had been the unity of natural force, and now that clue seemed to quiver under a new, unnamed energy.

Chicago, for the first time, asked whether the American people knew where they were driving. Adams answered that he did not, but would try to find out; and, since the Fair was the first expression of American thought as a unity, one must start there.

Washington was the second. He fell headlong into the extra session to repeal the Silver Act. The dealers in exchange insisted on the single gold standard; parties divided along capitalistic lines, with rare exceptions; the temper was better than usual; the end, comedy. On the evening of the vote, Senators came home gay, as if they had shifted a weight. Adams too felt light, a bystander who had stood up for his eighteenth century—Constitution, Pilgrims, Quincy and Harvard—by habit and taste till he found himself alone, hugging his antiquated dislike of bankers till he became little better than a crank. The people settled it at last. Between 1793 and 1893 the country had swayed between two forces; now the majority declared once for all in favor of the capitalistic system and its machinery. Friends, churches, colleges, the educated classes joined the banks to force submission by the mere law of mass. Of all régimes this was the one he liked least, but his likings were as antiquated as State rights. The system adopted must be run by its own methods; nothing could exceed the nonsense of trying to drive so concentrated a machine by Western farmers in alliance with city day-laborers.

The vote came; the gold standard won; and Adams, with his eighteenth-century prejudices, accepted that the capitalistic system had absorbed his class along with the rest, leaving only the question how long and how far its acceleration would run.

## Chapter 3

The convulsion of 1893 left its victims in dead-water. For connecting the nineteenth with the twentieth century the four years 1893–1897 had little value in education; much that had made life pleasant between 1870 and 1890 perished in the ruin, and among the earliest wreckage lay the fortunes of Clarence King. In 1871 Adams had thought King’s education ideal, his fitness unrivalled; after twenty years the scientific scheme failed where most theory fails—for want of money. Education without capital could always be taken by the throat and forced to disgorge its gains; the weak holder was sure to be frozen out. Adams himself, who fancied he stood outside risk, had hung for months over bankruptcy, saved only because the whole class of millionaires were more or less bankrupt too, and the banks must let mice escape with the rats.

If success were the test, it was not the man of science that passed, but the administrator with mediæval energies and no education beyond his branch. As types within reach, Adams looked at Hay, Reid, and Whitney, who owed their free hand to marriage, education serving for ornament. Newspapers might exhaust the commonplaces of wealth; New York neither respected nor much envied its very rich; yet Whitney was palpably envied; he had thrown aside the usual toys of ambition like ashes of smoked cigarettes and gone on gorging appetite upon appetite till even Europe was but an annex to his will. He had succeeded where King failed. Society had discovered no education that suited it best.

Had Adams been starting again in 1894, as in 1854, he would still have asked only the four old tools—mathematics, French, German, Spanish—against nine rivals in ten. King’s breakdown, physical as well as financial, brought the indirect gain that, on recovering strength, he dragged Adams to Cuba. Santiago and the buzzards on the trade-wind amused; the danza and the colors at sunrise asked no loftier study; but, as though they were still twenty and revolution young, the fabric fell on their heads. The rebellion severed the last tie that held Adams to a Democratic administration. He thought the President could have settled Cuba without war and would not; with the gold standard and the laws of mass, the old organization broke; the American had turned his back on the nineteenth century before he was done with it, and the movement, once accelerated, crushed good and bad alike.

For another year he lingered on the outskirts among picturesque, primitive types that were the more amusing for their torpor: winter islands, summer Rockies with Hay, where the bears were friendly and the hunters humane; then northwestward to the last railways, then Mexico and the Gulf. Twenty thousand miles later he began to think he knew enough of the edges of life. They educate only artists; and as sixty approached, the artist died; a certain cerebral restlessness survived that no longer answered to sensual stimulant; one was driven from beauty to beauty as though art were a trotting-match.

Accepting arithmetic for the alternative, he plunged into statistics at Washington. The Government poured out columns for the asking; Worthington Ford supplied methods as well as matter; for a while averages projected themselves as laws into the future. Yet the statisticians talked without faith; every increase of mass—volume and velocity—brought in new elements; a scholar fresh in arithmetic and ignorant of algebra fell into a superstitious terror of complexity, the sink of facts. One could frame no satisfactory answer to Adam Smith’s constructiveness, to Marx’s destructiveness, to the anarchist’s imprecations; societies that violated every law—not only moral and economical but arithmetical—propagated and multiplied complexities with every propagation.

The human factor was worse. Since the day of Pteraspis nothing had so confused the student as fin-de-siècle conduct. Wars were almost continuous; massacres counted only by the hundred-thousand drew notice; greed plundered with Roman crudity; murder seemed archaic, yet chronic. In perplexity he turned to the religious press; as an agent of motion he preferred the vigor of the shark; from his aching consciousness of religious void he doubted whether any large fraction of society cared for a future life, or even for the present one thirty years hence.

The object of education changed. Having lost itself for years studying what the world had ceased to care for, it must try to find out what the mass did care for, and why. Religion, politics, statistics, travel led to nothing. Accidental education littered the memory with chance images till one might as well educate a gravel-pit. Worse than futile, it grew ridiculous. For the moment, as so often before, a woman rescued him. Towards midsummer, 1895, Mrs. Lodge bade him follow her to Europe with the Senator and the boys.

The study of history teaches chiefly one’s ignorance of women; the American woman will live only as the man saw her; but she was better company than the man. With the Lodges in Normandy—Caen, Coutances, Mont-Saint-Michel—Adams, who had thought himself at home in the twelfth and thirteenth centuries, found his playgrounds turn green and deep as virgin forest. Through younger eyes the old problem became new and personal; the German lecture-room fell away; by an unwarned instinct the atmosphere of 1200 made even a Senator natural and liberal. The novelty expelled the pedantry once for all. He drifted back to Washington with a new sense of history; south again to Mexico; in May, a rapid run with Hay as far as Ravenna; then home in October with the rest to elect McKinley and start the world anew.

For the old world of public men and measures since 1870 he had no tears, and neither had the public; but in a small society like Washington the natural result of such indifference was to lean abjectly on intimacies. Life narrowed to the houses about La Fayette Square. Then Mr. McKinley entered the White House and in a moment tore the slow-built nest to bits. Hay took orders for London; others scattered; Adams found himself alone. Worse, to one whose interest lay in foreign affairs amid Cuban, Hawaiian, Nicaraguan chaos, the man in the State Department seemed more vital than the President. Hearing that Mr. McKinley meant to put John Sherman into State in order to make a place in the Senate, Adams felt shocked beyond restraints, not less for the betrayal of an old friend—Sherman was senile—than for the Department. One might have acquiesced had the President named the Senator-maker his Secretary, for force may serve where experience fails; but Sherman must tragically break down. Hints that Hay might be called when Sherman retired did not improve it; had Hay even unconsciously shared such an intrigue, Adams would have washed his hands of public affairs for good. Washington became uninhabitable. Once more, one must go!

Nothing was easier. On April 21, 1897, he reached London, where Queen Victoria still reigned and St. James’s Street looked much as it did when he first saw it. Yet Carlton House Terrace squeaked with ghosts; he felt like Odysseus, daunted by a bloodless fear. Slipping off to Paris, he set up at St. Germain, taught and learned French history for nieces under the venerable cedars, rode the green alleys. Summer ran smooth until the Hays came by, and Mrs. Hay, ally of twenty years, bade him go to Egypt.

He cared little to see Egypt again but gladly drifted after Hay to the Nile. They said and saw as little as possible of education until, at Assouan, came a telegram: the Maine blown up in Havana Harbor. The greatest stride in education since 1865—what did it teach? Leaning on a column-stump in the great hall at Karnak, he watched a jackal creep down the ruin. The brute’s ancestors had crept there when the wall was building; what was his view of the value of silence? He lay in the sands and watched the Sphinx. Brooks had taught him that the relation between civilizations is trade. Henry wandered, or was storm-driven, down the coast; tried to trace the harbor of Ephesus; crossed to Athens, picked up Rockhill, hunted Tiryns; together they went on to Constantinople, studying the walls of Constantine and the domes of Justinian. His hobby had turned into a camel, and he hoped, riding long enough in silence along the great highways of exchange, to come at last on a city of thought.

Meanwhile the world preached silence to the elderly. Youth may betray its ignorance; age had best hold its tongue. All men praised silence—in others. “Even a fool,” said the wisest of men, “when he holdeth his peace, is counted wise.” Carlyle vociferated its praise; Matthew Arnold thought it the best form of expression; Swinburne, to the end, the most noble. Alfred de Vigny’s dying wolf murmured:

“A voir ce que l’on fut sur terre et ce qu’on laisse,
Seul le silence est grand; tout le reste est faiblesse.”

“When one thinks what one leaves in the world when one dies,
Only silence is strong,—all the rest is but lies.”

None of them, nor philosophy after them, had much faith in silence as a cure for their own ills; all affirmed that no man, even at sixty, had been known to attain knowledge, and that a very few were believed to have attained ignorance, which was the same. The hobby was set: the Pursuit of Ignorance in Silence. If anywhere the planet kept a haunt where futility reigned content, he would find it—by statistics or cathedrals, by jackals or domes, by steamship curves or a dynamo’s infant hum—though he must ride his camel to the world’s end.
